title: When It Comes to Disputes, Beginnings Predict Endings
author: Admired Leadership
summary: Argues that how a conflict starts largely determines how it ends, so the first minutes of a dispute set the tone for everything after. A harsh or accusatory opening is received as an attack, prompts an equally aggressive response, and quickly makes rational discussion nearly impossible. Leaders who start aggressively often do so because they feel upset or justified, but the result is the same. The remedy is to raise concerns gently, describe the problem without blame, and aim at working better together rather than winning. The more justified a leader feels, the more important a calm opening becomes.
points: Conflicts that begin aggressively tend to deteriorate and end with rancor, so the opening minutes matter most.
A harsh opening is perceived as an assault, which triggers defensive and equally aggressive replies.
Feeling justified is no excuse; the angrier the leader, the more important a smooth start.
Good leaders describe the problem calmly, explore it, and frame the goal as better future collaboration instead of proving the other party wrong.
Disciplining yourself to begin mildly raises the odds of a reasonable discussion.
quotes: The first few minutes of a dispute set the tone for the rest of the conversation. Conflicts that begin aggressively typically deteriorate quickly, and commonly end with rancor. Beginnings really matter.

Disputes that start with one party issuing a harsh or accusatory statement set a hugely negative tone. Those on the receiving end are often surprised by the severity of the opening and view it as an attack.
Once the leader begins aggressively, the likelihood of working through the issue fades quickly. Once a “fight” breaks out, it is almost impossible to engage reasonably and rationally.

By calmly stating or describing the problem without moving quickly to blame or accusation, the dispute has a great chance to proceed peacefully, without the need to resort to inflammatory language or statements. The more upset or justified a leader feels about an issue, the more important it is to get the conversation off to a smooth start.

They make the goal of any dispute about understanding how to work more productively with the other party in the future. Since they aren’t concerned with winning or proving the other party wrong, they are more likely to elevate their concerns more thoughtfully.

By disciplining themselves against a negative start and insisting that they begin a dispute more mildly, they increase the odds that reasonable discussion will ensue. A dispute that begins with a high temperature is likely to be a scorcher. There’s no upside in that.
